entry: Animation originating from [[Japan]]. Outside Japan and in English, the term refers specifically to animation produced in Japan, while in Japanese *anime* describes all animated works regardless of style or origin. The earliest commercial Japanese animation dates to 1917. A characteristic art style emerged in the 1960s with the work of cartoonist [[Osamu Tezuka]], and the medium developed a large domestic audience. Many series are adapted from [[Manga|manga]], light novels or [[Video game|video games]]. The industry includes over 430 production companies, among them [[Studio Ghibli]], Kyoto Animation, Sunrise and MAPPA. Since the 1980s the medium has seen widespread international success, and by 2022 anime had become one of the fastest-growing genres of content globally. Compared with Western animation, anime generally focuses less on movement and more on the detail of settings and on camera effects such as panning and zooming.

Worldview holding that natural phenomena, including non-human organisms, landforms and inanimate objects, possess spiritual essences, souls or personhood. It assumes that animals, plants, rivers, weather systems and other natural entities have some degree of agency, life and will. The term is used in the anthropology of [[Religion|religion]] for the beliefs of many [[Indigenous peoples]], in contrast to later organized religions. The term is an anthropological construct, and many indigenous peoples have no word for animism or even for religion. Edward Tylor defined it in his 1871 book *Primitive Culture* as 'the general doctrine of souls and other spiritual beings in general'. Scholars disagree on whether animism describes an ancestral mode of experience shared by indigenous peoples or a religion in its own right. A 2016 comparative study found that animism was the oldest religious belief, present in the most recent common ancestor of hunter-gatherer groups.

Flowering plant of the family [[Apiaceae]], native to the Eastern Mediterranean and Southwest Asia. Its seeds have flavor and aroma similarities with star anise, [[Fennel]], [[Liquorice|liquorice]] and tarragon. Anise was first cultivated in the [[Middle East]], and it has been cultivated in Egypt for approximately 4,000 years. It is widely used to flavor food, candy and alcoholic drinks, especially around the Mediterranean, and its seeds are used in teas and regional confectionery. The main flavor component of its essential oil, anethole, is also found in star anise, an unrelated spice from South China that has largely displaced anise in Western markets. Anise is a food plant for the larvae of some [[Lepidoptera]] species, including the lime-speck pug.

American actress known for portraying eccentric and distinctive characters. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for her role as a mobster's moll in *Prizzi's Honor* (1985), directed by her father, John Huston. Her other films include *Crimes and Misdemeanors* (1989), *The Grifters* (1990) and the *Addams Family* films (1991–93), in which she played Morticia Addams. She won a Golden Globe for playing Carrie Chapman Catt in the cable film *Iron Jawed Angels* (2004). She also directed *Bastard Out of Carolina* (1996).

Capital city of [[Turkey]], in central [[Anatolia]]. Its urban center has a population of over 5.3 million, and Ankara Province has 6 million residents. Ankara is Turkey's second-largest city after [[Istanbul]]. Known in antiquity as Ancyra, it served as capital of the Celtic state of Galatia (280–64 BC) and of a Roman province. The Ottomans made it the capital of the Anatolia Eyalet (1393 – late 15th century), the Angora Eyalet (1827–1864) and the Angora Vilayet (1867–1922). On 23 April 1920 the Grand National Assembly of Turkey was established in Ankara, which became the headquarters of the Turkish National Movement during the [[Turkish War of Independence]]. Ankara became the new Turkish capital upon the establishment of the Republic on 29 October 1923, succeeding the former Ottoman capital Istanbul after the fall of the [[Ottoman Empire]]. The city is an important commercial and industrial center, and it is home to numerous universities.

Genus of armored [[Dinosaur|dinosaur]] from the very end of the [[Cretaceous]] Period, in western North America. Its [[Fossil|fossils]] date from 70–66 million years ago. Named by Barnum Brown in 1908, it is monotypic, containing only *A. magniventris*. Possibly the largest known ankylosaurid, it was between 6 and 8 m (20 and 26 ft) long. Its body was covered in armor plates, and its tail ended in a large club, probably used in defense against predators. Specimens have been found in the Hell Creek Formation, in [[Montana]], and it lived alongside [[Tyrannosaurus]] and [[Triceratops]].

Russian and Soviet poet, born Anna Andreyevna Gorenko. She was born in a resort suburb of the [[Black Sea]] port of Odessa, then in the [[Russian Empire]] and now in [[Ukraine]]. Her style, marked by economy and emotional restraint, was strikingly original. Her cycle *Requiem* (1935–40) is about the Stalinist terror. Her work was condemned and censored by Stalinist authorities, and she chose not to emigrate, remaining in the [[Soviet Union]] as a witness to events around her. Her first husband, Nikolai Gumilev, was executed by the Cheka, and her son Lev Gumilev and her common-law husband Nikolay Punin spent many years in the [[Gulag]], where Punin died. Her early work (1912–25) and later work (from about 1936) were divided by a decade of reduced literary output. She was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1965 and 1966.

Austrian-born British psychoanalyst. She was the sixth and youngest child of [[Sigmund Freud]] and Martha Bernays, born in [[Vienna]], [[Austria-Hungary]]. She followed her father into [[Psychoanalysis|psychoanalysis]] and, with Hermine Hug-Hellmuth and Melanie Klein, is considered a founder of psychoanalytic child psychology. Her work emphasized the ego and its normal 'developmental lines', and it drew on collaborative work in analytical and observational settings. After the family were forced to leave Vienna in 1938 under the Nazi regime, she resumed her practice in London. There she established the Hampstead Child Therapy Course and Clinic in 1952, later renamed the Anna Freud National Centre for Children and Families.

Novel by [[Leo Tolstoy]], first published in book form in 1878. It was serialized from 1875 to 1877, mostly in the periodical *The Russian Messenger*. Often considered among the greatest works of world literature, it centers on an extramarital affair between Anna and the [[Cavalry|cavalry]] officer Count Alexei Vronsky, which scandalizes [[Saint Petersburg]] society and forces the couple to flee to Italy. After they return to Russia, their lives further unravel. The novel deals with betrayal, faith, family, marriage and the differences between rural and urban life, and [[Train|trains]] recur as a motif. The story is set against the liberal reforms of [[Alexander II of Russia|Emperor Alexander II]]. It has been adapted to theater, opera, film, television, ballet, figure skating and radio drama.

American model, actress and television personality. She became a [[Playboy]] centerfold in May 1992 and was named 1993 Playmate of the Year. In 1994 she married the billionaire J. Howard Marshall, who was 89 years old. After his death in 1995 she began a lengthy legal battle over his estate that reached the [[Supreme Court of the United States]]. She starred in the E! reality program *The Anna Nicole Show* (2002–2004). She died of combined drug intoxication in Hollywood, Florida.

New Zealand actress. Born in [[Winnipeg]], Canada, and raised in [[Wellington]], she won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress at age 11 for *The Piano* (1993), becoming the second-youngest winner in Oscar history. She played Rogue in the *X-Men* franchise (2000–2006, 2014). She played the lead role of Sookie Stackhouse in the [[HBO]] vampire drama *True Blood* (2008–2014), for which she won a Golden Globe Award for Best Actress in 2009.

Russian prima ballerina. Born in [[Saint Petersburg]], she was accepted into the Imperial Ballet School at age 10 and studied with Enrico Cecchetti, considered the greatest ballet virtuoso of the time. Her passion for ballet began after seeing [[Marius Petipa]]'s original production of *The Sleeping Beauty*. At the Imperial Theatres she performed in ballets including *La Camargo*, *Le Roi Candaule*, *Marcobomba* and *The Sleeping Beauty*. She was a principal artist of the Imperial Russian [[Ballet|ballet]] and of Sergei Diaghilev's Ballets Russes, but she is most recognized for creating the role of *The Dying Swan*. With her own company, she was the first ballerina to tour the world, including South America, India, [[Mexico]] and Australia.

British-American media executive. She was editor of [[Vogue (magazine)|British Vogue]] from 1985 to 1987, then editor-in-chief of the American edition from 1988 to 2025, reviving what many saw as a stagnating publication. She is praised for identifying emerging fashion trends but criticized for a reportedly aloof and demanding personality. She is global chief content officer and artistic director at Condé Nast. Wintour has chaired the annual Met Gala in [[Manhattan]] since the 1990s. Animal rights activists have attacked her for promoting fur. The character Miranda Priestly in *The Devil Wears Prada* (2006) is believed to be based on her.

Mountain in the Annapurna range of north-central [[Nepal]], the 10th highest in the world. At 8,091 meters (26,545 ft) above sea level, it is notable for the difficulty and danger of its ascent. In 1950 a French expedition led by Maurice Herzog climbed it by the north face, the first eight-thousander to be successfully climbed. The surrounding area lies within the 7,629 sq km Annapurna Conservation Area, the first and largest in Nepal. As of February 2025 its fatality rate was 13.42% (75 deaths from 559 ascents), according to [[Guinness World Records]].

Orange-red [[Condiment|condiment]] and food coloring derived from the seeds of the achiote tree (*Bixa orellana*), native to tropical parts of the Americas. It imparts a yellow to red-orange color and may add a sweet, peppery flavor. The color comes mainly from [[Carotenoid|carotenoid]] pigments, bixin and norbixin. As a natural alternative to synthetic coloring, annatto is used in cheeses, [[Butter|butter]], [[Margarine|margarine]], [[Cake|cakes]], potatoes, snack foods, breakfast cereals and sausages, although it has been linked to rare food allergies.

American actress associated with method acting, having studied under Lee Strasberg at the Actors Studio. She won Tony Awards for her Broadway roles in *Two for the Seesaw* (1958) and *The Miracle Worker* (1959), and an Academy Award for Best Actress for the 1962 film version of *The Miracle Worker*. She is one of 24 thespians to achieve the Triple Crown of Acting. Born in the [[The Bronx|Bronx]], she was married to [[Mel Brooks]].

German-born Jewish diarist and [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]] victim. Born in [[Frankfurt]], she moved with her family to [[Amsterdam]] in 1934, after [[Adolf Hitler]] of the [[Nazi Party]] was appointed to govern Germany. As persecution of Jews increased, the family went into hiding in a secret annex in Amsterdam in July 1942. They were arrested by the [[Gestapo]] on 4 August 1944. Anne was transferred to the Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, where she died, presumably of [[Typhus|typhus]], in February or March 1945. Her diary, written in hiding, was published in 1947 by her father, Otto Frank, the only family member to survive. It appeared in English in 1952 as *The Diary of a Young Girl* and has been translated into over 70 languages.

American actress. Her breakthrough came as Mia Thermopolis in the Disney comedy *The Princess Diaries* (2001). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing Fantine in *Les Misérables* (2012). She played Selina Kyle, or Catwoman, in *The Dark Knight Rises* (2012), the first of three films with director [[Christopher Nolan]]. Her films have grossed more than $6.7 billion worldwide. She won a Primetime Emmy Award for a guest voice role on *The Simpsons*, and she advocates for [[Gender equality|gender equality]] as a UN Women Goodwill Ambassador.

British crime writer. She wrote the Thomas and Charlotte Pitt and William Monk series of historical [[Detective fiction|detective fiction]]. In 1994 it became public that she had been convicted of murder in [[Christchurch]], New Zealand, in 1954, when she was 15. She and her friend Pauline Parker had killed Parker's mother, Honorah. After serving a five-year sentence she changed her name from Juliet Hulme and returned to the United Kingdom. Her identity was made public after the film *Heavenly Creatures*, directed by [[Peter Jackson]] and based on the case, was released.

Queen of England, Scotland and Ireland (r. 1702–14), and of Great Britain from 1707. She was the last monarch of the House of Stuart. Her father, James, had been deposed in the [[Glorious Revolution]] of 1688. Anne favored moderate Tory politicians, but the Whigs grew more powerful during the [[War of the Spanish Succession]] until 1710, when she dismissed many of them from office. Plagued by poor health, she grew increasingly ill and obese. Despite 17 pregnancies, she died without surviving issue. She was succeeded by George I of the House of Hanover under the Act of Settlement 1701, which excluded Catholics from the succession.

American author of Gothic fiction, erotic literature and Bible fiction. She is best known for *The Vampire Chronicles*, which began with *Interview with the Vampire* (1976). Its 1994 film adaptation was a commercial success. Following a publicized return to Catholicism in the mid-2000s, she wrote novels about the life of [[Jesus]], including *Christ the Lord: Out of Egypt*. Born in [[New Orleans]], she later lived in Texas and San Francisco. Her books have sold over 100 million copies.

Novel by the Canadian author Lucy Maud Montgomery, published in 1908. Written for all ages, it follows Anne Shirley, an 11-year-old orphan sent by mistake to the middle-aged siblings Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert, who had intended to adopt a boy to help on their farm, Green Gables, in the fictional town of Avonlea on [[Prince Edward Island]]. The book has been translated into at least 36 languages and has sold more than 50 million copies. It was the first of many novels in the series, and it has been adapted as films, television series and musicals.

Phylum of segmented worms, including ragworms, [[Earthworm|earthworms]] and [[Leech|leeches]]. The phylum has over 22,000 extant species, living in marine environments from tidal zones to [[Hydrothermal vent|hydrothermal vents]], in fresh water and on land. The basic body form is a series of segments called metameres, and most [[Polychaete|polychaetes]] have paired parapodia for locomotion. Traditional divisions into polychaetes, oligochaetes and leech-like hirudineans were revised from 1997, when cladistic research began treating leeches as a subgroup of oligochaetes. Annelids improve [[Soil fertility|soil fertility]] and are monitored by scientists as indicators of water quality. Some leech species are endangered after overharvesting for [[Bloodletting|bloodletting]]. Because annelids are soft-bodied, their fossils are rare; the oldest confidently identified fossil is about 518 million years old, from the early [[Cambrian]].

American exhibition shooter and folk heroine. Raised in poverty in western Ohio, she hunted as a child to help support her family. At 15 she won a shooting contest against the marksman Frank E. Butler, whom she married in 1876. The pair joined Buffalo Bill's Wild West in 1885 and performed in Europe before royalty. After a rail accident in 1901 she took a less taxing routine and taught women marksmanship. Her stage acts were filmed for one of [[Thomas Edison|Thomas Edison's]] earliest Kinetoscopes in 1894. Her story was adapted for stage musicals and films, including *Annie Get Your Gun*.

Calendar era dating years from the traditionally reckoned year of the conception or birth of [[Jesus]]. Anno Domini (AD) and before Christ (BC) qualify years in the [[Gregorian calendar|Gregorian]] and [[Julian calendar|Julian]] calendars, and there is no year zero. Medieval [[Latin|Latin]] for 'in the year of the Lord', the system was devised in 525 by the Eastern Roman monk Dionysius Exiguus, but it was not widely used until the 9th century. Modern scholars believe that Jesus was born about 5 BC. Many writers prefer [[Common Era|CE]] and BCE to avoid religious associations.
